title: Arrays & Tuples
subtitle: Typed arrays, readonly, and fixed-length tuples
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: A JavaScript array can hold values of any type — [1, 'hello', true] is valid. This makes it easy to accidentally mix types or access elements that don't exist.
whyItExists.solution: TypeScript lets you type arrays to hold only one type: number[], or string[]. Tuples let you define fixed-length arrays where each position has its own type — [string, number] for a [name, age] pair.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Type arrays whenever you know all elements share a type. Use tuples for structured pairs/triples where position has meaning (coordinates, key-value pairs, function return values).
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't use tuples for long structures — use interfaces or objects instead. Tuples lose their positional meaning beyond 3-4 elements.

explainModes.beginner: number[] means 'an array that can only contain numbers'. string[] means 'array of strings only'. A tuple [string, number] is like a fixed-size box where slot 0 must be a string and slot 1 must be a number — useful for things like [name, score] pairs.
explainModes.simple: Array types: number[], string[], boolean[]. Generic form: Array<string> (same thing). Readonly: readonly number[] or ReadonlyArray<number> — can't push/pop. Tuple: [string, number] — exactly 2 elements with those types. Named tuple: [name: string, age: number]. Rest in tuple: [string, ...number[]] — one string then any number of numbers. Destructuring with types.
explainModes.standard: const assertion: const colors = ['red', 'blue'] as const — type is readonly ['red', 'blue'], not string[]. This prevents mutation and narrows the type to the literal values. Tuple spread: [...tuple1, ...tuple2]. Array.isArray() narrows to any[]. Type predicates (is) for narrowing to typed arrays. Multi-dimensional arrays: number[][] or string[][].
explainModes.technical: Array<T> is generic syntax equivalent to T[]. TypeScript's Array type is covariant: string[] is assignable to (string | number)[] but not vice versa. Tuple types are subtypes of their corresponding array types: [string, number] is assignable to (string | number)[]. Variadic tuple types (TS 4.0): function concat<T extends unknown[], U extends unknown[]>(a: [...T], b: [...U]): [...T, ...U] — combines tuple types.
explainModes.deepDive: Labeled tuple elements improve readability and IDE display: type Coordinate = [x: number, y: number, z?: number]. Optional elements in tuples (trailing only): [string, number?]. Rest elements in tuples: [string, ...number[]] matches ['a', 1, 2, 3]. Tuples are the backbone of TypeScript's inferring from function arguments: Parameters<typeof fn> extracts a function's parameter types as a tuple. ReturnType<typeof fn> extracts the return type.

questions.question: What does `const data: [string, number]` mean?
options: An array of strings and numbers mixed together
A tuple: exactly 2 elements — first a string, second a number
An array that can have either strings or numbers at any position
A type error — you can't mix types in an array
questions.explanation: [string, number] is a tuple type — a fixed-length array where position 0 must be a string and position 1 must be a number. data[0] is always string, data[1] is always number. TypeScript will error if you try to assign a wrong type to either position or add extra elements.

faq.q: When should I use a tuple vs an object?
faq.a: Tuples work well for 2-3 element structures where order is the convention (coordinates [x, y], divmod result [quotient, remainder]). Beyond 3 elements, or when the structure has named fields, use an interface or object: { x: number, y: number } is clearer than [number, number] when there are many fields.
